objective: Build a text adventure game in Python that is genuinely fun to play. The engine loads world data from YAML files defining rooms, items, NPCs, monsters, and connections. Implement a command parser handling movement (go north/south/east/west), inventory management (take, drop, use, examine), NPC interaction (talk to), combat commands (attack, flee), and look/status/help/quit. Add a turn-based combat system: the player has health and attack power, weapons and armor found in the world change combat stats when equipped, healing items can be used mid-fight, and monsters guard specific rooms and fight back with simple distinct behaviors. Include a final boss with two phases and a weakness to a special item hidden in the world — beating the boss wins the game, and dying ends the run with an honest defeat screen and the option to restart. Manage game state including player location, stats, equipment, inventory, room state changes, NPC dialogue progression, and defeated monsters. Support save and load of full game state to JSON. Create a playable demo world with at least 8 rooms, 5 items (including at least one weapon, one armor piece, one healing item, and the boss-weakness item), 2 NPCs with branching dialogue that hints at the boss weakness, 3 regular monsters, and the final boss. The game must be runnable from the command line, produce engaging descriptive text with clear combat narration, and be winnable in a reasonable playthrough by following the NPC hints.

Create world.yaml with content: Design an adventurous ruined citadel called the "Echoing Keep" with at least eight interconnected rooms: a Crumbling Gatehouse, Dusty Courtyard, Whispering Library, Forgotten Armory, Sunlit Atrium, Shadowed Catacombs, Mystic Sanctum, and the Throne of the Fallen King (final boss arena). Populate the world with five memorable items: a rusted Sword of Dawn (weapon that raises player attack), a battered Breastplate of Echoes (armor that raises defense), a Healing Herb Pouch (restores health when used), a Crystal Shard of Light (the unique item that exploits the final boss's weakness), and a Lantern of Guidance (helps reveal hidden passages). Include two NPCs with branching dialogue: an old Scholar who dwells in the Whispering Library, offering lore about the citadel and subtly hinting that "light can shatter the king's shadow" (pointing to the Crystal Shard), and a weary Guard stationed at the Dusty Courtyard who warns of a relentless guardian and mentions that a special relic hidden deep can turn the tide. Add three regular monsters: a Skeletal Warrior roaming the Forgotten Armory, a Swarm of Bats in the Shadowed Catacombs, and a Stone Golem protecting the Mystic Sanctum, each with simple distinct combat behaviors. Finally, craft a two‑phase Final Boss – the Fallen King – who initially fights with heavy melee attacks, then, when his health drops below half, shifts to a shadowy phase vulnerable only to the Crystal Shard of Light. The world data should also define the connections between rooms, which items are located where, NPC locations, and which monsters guard specific rooms.
Program starts cleanly and exits without errors
User can move between connected rooms using movement commands and see the room description
User can examine items in a room and take them, adding them to the inventory
User can use a healing item during combat to restore health
Player can attack a monster and deal damage based on equipped weapon stats
User can talk to an NPC and receive branching dialogue that provides hints
Final boss changes phase when health drops below half and becomes vulnerable only to the special item, which can be used to defeat it
User can save the current game state to a JSON file and later load it, restoring all progress

notes.content:
Import scheme: flat. Run: python main.py. Smoke: echo quit | python main.py. Files: entities.py, world_loader.py, parser.py, combat.py, state.py, save_load.py, main.py.
Data shapes:
  world.yaml → world_loader.py: Top-level mapping with keys rooms, items, npcs, monsters; each maps IDs to definitions with required fields.
State contracts:
  Player (owner entities.py, consumers state.py, combat.py, parser.py, main.py): location: str (room_id); health: int; max_health: int; attack: int; defense: int; inventory: list of item_id strings; equipped_weapon: str or null; equipped_armor: str or null
  GameState (owner state.py, consumers main.py, save_load.py): player: Player dict; rooms_state: mapping room_id -> {visited: bool, items: list of item_id strings, monsters: list of monster_id strings, npcs: list of npc_id strings}; npcs_dialogue_progress: mapping npc_id -> int (next dialogue index); monsters_state: mapping monster_id -> {health: int, phase: int (for boss)}
  savegame.json (owner save_load.py, consumers load_game, save_game): JSON representation of GameState (same fields as GameState schema).

Use a data‑driven architecture: store every world element (rooms, items, NPCs, monsters, connections) in separate YAML files and load them at startup with a single loader that validates the structure (e.g., using PyYAML together with pydantic models). Represent each entity as a lightweight class that holds only its static attributes; mutable state (player location, inventory, monster health, NPC dialogue flags, room “visited” or “cleared” markers) should live in a central `GameState` object that can be serialized to JSON for save/load. Keep the loader read‑only and let the game engine modify only the `GameState`, which avoids accidental overwriting of world definitions when saving.

Implement the command parser as a table‑driven dispatcher: map verb strings (`go`, `take`, `drop`, `use`, `examine`, `talk`, `attack`, `flee`, `look`, `status`, `help`, `quit`) to handler functions that receive the current `GameState` and any arguments. For movement, resolve direction strings against the room’s adjacency map; for inventory actions, enforce capacity limits and automatically equip weapons/armor when taken (updating player attack/defense stats). Combat should be a turn loop that alternates between player and monster actions, using simple deterministic formulas (`damage = attacker.attack - defender.defense`, minimum 1) and allowing healing items to be used mid‑fight. Encode monster behavior as a small state machine (e.g., “aggressive”, “defensive”, “flee”) so each type can have distinct attack patterns without duplicating code.

Design the final boss as a composite object with two phases: phase 1 uses normal stats, phase 2 is triggered when health drops below a threshold and swaps in a new set of attacks and higher defense. Store the boss’s weakness as a special item flag; the combat handler should check for that flag and apply extra damage or bypass a defense layer when the player possesses the item. Hook NPC dialogue to set a boolean on the `GameState` (e.g., `hints_given`) and optionally reveal the weakness after a specific conversation branch, ensuring the hint is only shown once. When saving, dump the entire `GameState` (including player stats, inventory, room flags, monster HP, and boss phase) to JSON; on load, reconstruct the state and re‑link entity references by ID. Common pitfalls: mixing static world data with mutable state (which corrupts saves), hard‑coding command strings inside handlers (making extensions painful), and allowing combat loops to run without a break condition (causing infinite hangs). Guard against these by keeping YAML immutable, using a central dispatch table, and always checking for victory/defeat after each turn.
